name: Parsnip
grown_as: The garden parsnip, a biennial grown as an annual for its long cream root, sown in spring and lifted from autumn through winter. Varieties differ little in leaf and flower.
habit: Year 1: an upright tuft of large leaves 40 to 60 cm high from the top of one long root. Year 2: a stout, hollow, sharply ridged and grooved flowering stem 1 to 1.5 m tall, branched near the top. The sap can burn skin in sunlight.

leaf.arrangement: A rosette from the crown at the top of the root
leaf.type: Compound: once pinnate, with 2 to 7 pairs of leaflets set opposite along the stalk and one at the end
leaf.leaflets: Leaflets without stalks or on very short ones, set well apart. Each broadly oval, often cut into two or three lobes at the base; the end leaflet usually three-lobed
leaf.outline: Whole leaf long-oval, 20 to 50 cm; leaflets 3 to 8 cm, oval to broadly oblong
leaf.base: Leaflet bases rounded to blunt, often lopsided; the leaf stalk sheathing the crown at its base
leaf.tip: Leaflets blunt to rounded at the tip
leaf.margin: Lobed and coarsely, irregularly toothed all round the leaflet, the teeth blunt to rounded
leaf.veins: A midrib with pinnate side veins, pressed in a little; netted
leaf.surface: Rather rough with short hairs, especially beneath; dull. Smells of parsnip when crushed
leaf.stalk: Long, grooved, hollow, hairy, widening to a sheath
leaf.colour: Yellowish mid green, paler than carrot

flower.form: A flat or slightly domed compound umbel of many tiny yellow flowers
flower.petals: Five free, tiny, yellow petals with tips rolled inward, all the same size (no enlarged outer petals)
flower.centre: Five yellow stamens and a yellow swollen disc in each flower; no dark central flower
flower.behind: No bracts or bracteoles, or one or two that soon fall: the spokes rise bare
flower.carried: Umbels of 5 to 15 spokes at the stem and branch tips, facing up
flower.size: Flowers about 2 mm; umbels 5 to 10 cm across
flower.season: June to August of the second year

fruit: Each pair of seeds a flat, oval to round, papery disc about 5 to 8 mm, with a narrow pale wing all round and a few dark thin oil lines running down the face. Straw-brown when ripe, held in an open umbel on bare spokes.
seedling: Two narrow strap-shaped seed leaves, 2 to 3 cm, longer and broader than a carrot's, then a first true leaf that is a single lobed leaflet, then leaves with leaflets in pairs. Slow to come up, often 3 to 4 weeks.
winter: The leaves die back and yellow in hard frost, leaving the crown at soil level with a few dead stalks; the roots are left in the ground and lifted as needed.

leaf: once pinnate: pairs of broad lobed leaflets along one stalk and one at the end
leaflets oval, coarsely toothed and lobed all round
bloom: a flat umbel of tiny yellow flowers on bare spokes
all petals the same small size
seed: a flat oval papery disc with a narrow pale wing
thin dark lines running down the face
seedling: a first true leaf with broad lobes, not finely cut
young: an upright tuft of pinnate leaves from one point, no stem
crop: a long cream-white root with broad shoulders, tapering to a thin point
a sunken crown at the top where the leaves arise
faint rings and fine side roots
flower: a tall grooved stem with pinnate leaves
flat yellow umbels at the branch tips
seedhead: open umbels of flat, round, straw-brown winged seeds

look_alikes: Wild parsnip is the same species with a thin root. Carrot has finely cut feathery leaves and white flowers with forked bracts. Alexanders has glossy leaves divided in threes and yellow-green flowers. Hogweed has white flowers and much larger, rougher leaves. Celery and celeriac have glossy leaves and greenish-white flowers.
